project_or_policy_name: Coastal Virginia Offshore Wind Project (City of Virginia Beach)
short_description: In 2020, Dominion Energy proposed the Coastal Virginia Offshore Wind Project, a 2,600-MW offshore wind farm.
long_description: In 2020, Dominion Energy proposed the Coastal Virginia Offshore Wind Project, a 2,600-MW offshore wind farm. In March 2024, the Committee for a Constructive Tomorrow, Heartland Institute, and National Legal and Policy Center filed a lawsuit in the U.S. District Court for the District of Columbia to halt the project. The lawsuit alleged that the construction would threaten the endangered North Atlantic right whale and that Dominion had not taken sufficient steps to protect right whales. The lawsuit further alleged that, when it approved the project, the Bureau of Ocean Energy Management (BOEM) failed to consider the cumulative impacts of offshore wind farms on the right whale population in violation of the Endangered Species Act. The plaintiffs moved for a preliminary injunction to halt the project’s construction until the National Marine Fisheries Service issues a new biological opinion. In May 2024, the court denied the request for preliminary injunction, stating that the plaintiffs failed to demonstrate that they would suffer irreparable harm and to account for the extensive measures to protect whales already in place. Separately, residents of Virginia Beach have raised concerns about vibrations, scenic disruptions, and environmental harm from the Coastal Virginia Offshore Wind Project. Dominion has stated that it has provided multiple opportunities for residents to engage with the company and that it is implementing measures to address their concerns. On December 22, 2025, the Bureau of Ocean Energy Management (BOEM) issued a stop-work order to halt the construction of the project for reasons of national security. The next day, on December 23, 2025, the developer filed a lawsuit in the U.S. District Court for the Eastern District of Virginia to enjoin BOEM’s stop-work order. In January 2026, the federal district judge granted the plaintiff’s request for a preliminary injunction and allowed construction of the project to resume.

project_or_policy_name: Apple Hill Solar and Willow Road Solar, f/k/a Chelsea Solar
short_description: Allco Renewable Energy’s plans for the 2-MW Apple Hill project and 2-MW Willow Road project in Bennington, Vermont have faced opposition from neighbors for close to a decade.
long_description: Allco Renewable Energy’s plans for the 2-MW Apple Hill project and 2-MW Willow Road project in Bennington, Vermont have faced opposition from neighbors for close to a decade. The state Public Utility Commission (PUC) initially approved the Apple Hill project in 2018, but opponents of the project appealed the decision, and the PUC reversed its own decision on remand in May 2020. In addition, in June 2019, the PUC denied a certificate of public good for the Willow Road project, finding that the Willow Road project and the Apple Hill project were in fact a single 4-MW solar plant and therefore ineligible under a state program for solar projects of 2.2 MW or less; the Vermont Supreme Court upheld that determination in January 2020. In June 2020 the PUC issued a temporary restraining order after Vermonters for a Clean Environment filed comments alleging that the developer was clearing trees on the proposed sites and that endangered plant species were being disturbed. On May 16, 2022, the PUC once again denied a permit for Apple Hill solar. In January 2023, the Bennington Planning Commission unanimously recommended against finding that the revised Willow Road (f/k/a Chelsea) solar project was within a preferred site for solar facilities, and in June 2023, the Bennington Select Board rejected the proposal. In July 2023, Allco filed a lawsuit in state court against the town of Bennington seeking to force the town to declare the proposed site a preferred location for solar under the town’s Energy Plan guidelines. This lawsuit was dismissed for lack of jurisdiction, and Allco responded by stating that it would bring the lawsuit in federal court instead. In October 2023, the Vermont Supreme Court affirmed the PUC’s 2020 denial of a certificate of public convenience and necessity. On December 12, 2023, the Vermont Supreme Court denied Allco’s request for reargument. On June 3, 2025, in a special Town of Bennington Select Board meeting, the board voted 5-1 to ratify a settlement agreement in support of the project. The board agreed that the project site is a “preferred area,” not prominently visible on a hillside, does not violate the town plan and does not have “adverse regional impact.”

short_description: In July 2016, AllEarth Renewables proposed a single 2.2-MW wind turbine on a 450-acre dairy air farm in the Town of Holland, after winning a state contract.
long_description: In July 2016, AllEarth Renewables proposed a single 2.2-MW wind turbine on a 450-acre dairy air farm in the Town of Holland, after winning a state contract. The project was stymied by significant delays at the Public Utility Commission (“PUC”). In 2017, Governor Phil Scott set the most stringent decibel limits for wind turbines in the United States: 42 decibels in the daytime and 39 decibels at night, as measured 100 feet from residences nearest to the turbines. In May 2018, the PUC issued a “bifurcation order” splitting the application requirements and further delaying progress. In January 2020, the developer announced that it was dropping plans for the project, blaming the Governor for opposition to wind energy and for appointing opponents of wind energy to the PUC. The Town of Holland actively fought the project, incurring more than $70,000 in legal fees over three years. In March 2020, the PUC dismissed the developer’s petition to build the project. short_description: The 85-acre, 20-MW Shaftsbury Solar project, proposed by Freepoint Commodities and SunEast Development LLC, has faced significant opposition in Bennington County.

long_description: A proposal to build the Viridis solar farm, a 300-acre, 50-MW project in the Town of Panton, has faced significant opposition from local residents. In Panton, a group of local residents have formed an organization called “No Mega Solar,” and approximately 300 people had signed paper petitions against the project as of May 2024. short_description: The Badger Mountain Solar Project is a 200-MW solar project proposed by Aurora Solar, LLC, a subsidiary of Avangrid Renewables, LLC.
long_description: The Badger Mountain Solar Project is a 200-MW solar project proposed by Aurora Solar, LLC, a subsidiary of Avangrid Renewables, LLC. Wenatchi-P’squosa people indigenous to the area have objected to the planned construction, citing concerns that the project threatens cultural resources including foodways and sacred sites on the mountain. In May 2023, the Confederated Tribes of the Colville Reservation formally registered their opposition to the project. In January 2024, ProPublica and High Country News published the results of an investigation that found that Washington State Department of Natural Resources’ process for assessing cultural resources had been inadequate. In August 2024, the developer announced that it was pausing project planning for 2 to 3 months as it re-evaluated public comments, including from project landowners and affected tribal nations

short_description: The proposed 160-MW Carriger Solar Project drew opposition from a group called Citizens Educated About Solar Energy (CEASE).
long_description: The proposed 160-MW Carriger Solar Project drew opposition from a group called Citizens Educated About Solar Energy (CEASE). In August 2021, the founder of CEASE was ejected from a public meeting about the project for causing a disruption. On January 10, 2023, the Klickitat County Commission adopted a 6-month moratorium on solar projects in the area where the project has been proposed. In August 2023, the Washington Energy Facility Site Evaluation Council (EFSEC) indicated that it was considering issuing a determination that the project would have “significant impacts” on the environment. Under Washington law, “significance” is defined as a “reasonably likelihood of more than a moderate adverse impact on environmental quality.” EFSEC identified two reasons for the adverse impacts: cultural impacts and visual aesthetics. On cultural impacts, EFSEC emphasized objections from the Yakama Nation centered on impacts to Traditional Cultural Properties (TCPs). The EFSEC also found it unlikely that mitigation efforts to lessen visual impacts would be effective. On June 26, 2025, the EFSEC issued a decision recommending that the Governor approve the project.
notes: Sabin 2026 entry 4342

short_description: Tuusso Energy applied to the State Energy Facility Site Evaluation Council (EFSEC) for permission to construct a 25-MW, 200-acre solar project across five parcels of private property.
long_description: Tuusso Energy applied to the State Energy Facility Site Evaluation Council (EFSEC) for permission to construct a 25-MW, 200-acre solar project across five parcels of private property. Neighbors of the site started an organization, Save Our Farms, to advocate against the project. short_description: The Yakama Nation has been fighting the proposed Goldendale Energy Storage Project on its ancestral land for five years due to concerns that the pumped storage project could destroy tribal cultural property.
long_description: The Yakama Nation has been fighting the proposed Goldendale Energy Storage Project on its ancestral land for five years due to concerns that the pumped storage project could destroy tribal cultural property. The project is planned to be constructed on a 680-acre site with the capacity to generate 1,200-MW of energy. On July 28, 2022, 17 of Washington State’s 29 federally recognized tribes sent a letter to Governor Inslee asking that he deny permits for the project. In February 2024, FERC released its final environmental review for the project, recommending the project move forward subject to certain conditions. Tribal nations have argued they were not properly consulted for the project and that the lack of consultation undermined FERC’s review of the project’s cultural impacts.

short_description: In June 2024, Tenaska submitted a proposal for a 200-MW battery energy storage system to the Energy Facility Site Evaluation Council (EFSEC) rather than seeking approval from Skagit County.
long_description: In June 2024, Tenaska submitted a proposal for a 200-MW battery energy storage system to the Energy Facility Site Evaluation Council (EFSEC) rather than seeking approval from Skagit County. The project is proposed to be located on approximately 16 acres zoned for agriculture in the outskirts of Sedro-Woolley. At a public hearing held in August 2024, local residents raised concerns of fire and environmental hazards. The Skagit County Commissioners, the Sedro-Woolley mayor and council, and District 39 state legislators all voiced their opposition to the project. In November 2024, the Skagit Board of County Commissioners amended the county development code to prohibit new electrical energy generation and storage on agricultural and resource land. In January 2025, District 39 Senator Keith Wagoner introduced Senate Bill 5283 to prohibit EFSEC from “preempting local laws that forbid the siting of certain storage facilities in critical areas.” In February 2025, EFSEC voted 3-2 that the project proposal was in compliance with the Skagit County development regulations that were in place at the time of application, allowing the proposal to move on to the State Environmental Policy Act review.
notes: Sabin 2026 entry 4345

short_description: On April 7, 2022, Cypress Creek Renewables submitted an application to the state EFSEC to construct the High Top and Ostrea Solar Project, which consists of two 80-MW components, High Top Solar and Ostrea Solar, each of which would cover 1,600 acres.
long_description: On April 7, 2022, Cypress Creek Renewables submitted an application to the state EFSEC to construct the High Top and Ostrea Solar Project, which consists of two 80-MW components, High Top Solar and Ostrea Solar, each of which would cover 1,600 acres. On July 26, 2022, the county imposed a moratorium on mid- and large-scale solar projects. In November 2022, the county commissioners sent two letters to the EFSEC asking the council to abide by the moratorium and hold off on approving any projects in the county until new local rules are finalized. However, in December 2022, the EFSEC informed the county commissioners that the EFSEC’s guiding laws “do not provide a mechanism to cease review of an [a]pplication . . . in light of a county-enacted moratorium.” In February 2023, the EFSEC approved the application for the project in spite of the county moratorium, sending the application on to Governor Inslee for final approval. short_description: Scout Clean Energy has proposed a 600-MW wind project on 24 miles of ridgeline on the Horse Heaven Hills.
long_description: Scout Clean Energy has proposed a 600-MW wind project on 24 miles of ridgeline on the Horse Heaven Hills. The project has garnered local opposition from groups such as Save Our Ridges, which maintains a website tracking the project. Construction was supposed to be finished by 2022, but the project was still under review as of August 2023. In August 2023, a hearing was scheduled for public comment about the proposed project. In September 2023, the Board of Benton County Commissioners published a resolution formally opposing the project. Opponents of the project have raised concerns about impacts to ferruginous hawks, as well as concerns about the cultural and historical significance of the Horse Heaven Hills to the Confederated Tribes and Bands of the Yakama Nation. The community group Tri-Cities C.A.R.E.S (Community Action for Responsible Environmental Stewardship) has also argued that the project will reduce property values and could obstruct emergency planes or hospitals in the event of wildfires. The state Energy Facility Site Evaluation Council (EFSEC) voted in April 2024 to recommend the Horse Heaven Project for approval over objections from the Yakama Nation. The EFSEC’s recommendation halved the Horse Heaven project’s size due to concerns that the facility would impact local endangered hawk populations. In May 2024, however, Governor Inslee rejected the proposal to halve the size of the project. In September 2024, the EFSEC approved a version of the project with mitigation measures that did not involve reducing the size of the project. Governor Inslee approved this version of the project in October 2024. In November 2024, Benton County, Tri-Cities CARES and the Yakama Nation each filed a separate lawsuit in the Thurston County Superior Court seeking judicial review of the approval by the state and the regulators and alleging irregularities and errors in the environmental impact study process.
notes: Sabin 2026 entry 4347; litigation venue: State

short_description: In 2002, SDS Lumber Company, dba Whistling Ridge Energy, LLC (“Whistling Ridge”) proposed the Whistling Ridge Energy Project as a 70-MW wind farm, with up to 85 wind turbines on both public and private land near the City of White Salmon in Klickitat County.
long_description: In 2002, SDS Lumber Company, dba Whistling Ridge Energy, LLC (“Whistling Ridge”) proposed the Whistling Ridge Energy Project as a 70-MW wind farm, with up to 85 wind turbines on both public and private land near the City of White Salmon in Klickitat County. The project faced immediate opposition from local residents, a conservation organization called Friends of the Columbia Gorge (“Friends”), and tourism groups, who raised concerns about poor project design and harm to scenic and wildlife resources. Over 400 public comments were submitted to the Energy Facility Site Evaluation Council (EFSEC), largely by opponents. In 2012, the Washington Department of Natural Resources denied the original project proposals but ultimately authorized a 10-year permit from 2012 to 2022 for up to 35 wind turbines. The Governor accepted the EFSEC’s recommendation and approved the project. In 2013, Friends challenged the approval in state court, which rejected their claims and affirmed the approval. In 2018, Friends filed a challenge in federal court, which also failed. However, the project was on hold until 2023, one year after the permit had expired. Whistling Ridge’s corporate successor, Twin Creeks Timber LLC filed a request to transfer ownership and extend the permit to 2026. However, in 2023, the EFSEC denied the requests, and the project was officially terminated.

short_description: The Cardinal-Hickory Creek Transmission Line is a 125-mile, 345-kilovolt transmission line that is planned to stretch from Dubuque County, Iowa to the Town of Middleton, Wisconsin.
long_description: The Cardinal-Hickory Creek Transmission Line is a 125-mile, 345-kilovolt transmission line that is planned to stretch from Dubuque County, Iowa to the Town of Middleton, Wisconsin. The transmission line is expected to support the interconnection of renewable energy generation in the upper Midwest region. The project has faced significant opposition. In 2021, the National Wildlife Refuge Association, the Driftless Area Land Conservancy, the Wisconsin Wildlife Federation, and the Defenders of Wildlife filed a series of lawsuits in the U.S. District Court for the Western District of Wisconsin. The lawsuits, which were consolidated, challenged the project under NEPA, the National Wildlife Refuge System Improvement Act, the Clean Water Act, and the Endangered Species Act. In November 2021, the federal district court granted a preliminary injunction preventing development of the project that would impact wetlands in southern Wisconsin’s Driftless Area. In January 2022, the federal district court held that federal approval of the project violated NEPA and the Refuge Act. Then, in July 2023, the Seventh Circuit Court of Appeals vacated the preliminary injunction and remanded the case for dismissal. In December 2023, the eastern half of the transmission line entered into service. In March 2024, the Driftless Area Land Conservancy, the National Wildlife Refuge Association, and the Wisconsin Wildlife Federation sued to block a federal land exchange necessary for the line’s crossing of a wildlife refuge along the Mississippi River. The U.S. District Court for the Western District of Wisconsin issued a preliminary injunction suspending federal approvals for the land exchange in March 2024, but in May 2024, the Seventh Circuit reversed the order, holding that the district court had not made the required finding that the movants were “likely to succeed on the merits.” The U.S. Fish & Wildlife Service completed the land exchange in May 2024. The transmission line completed construction and entered into full operation in September 2024, with the federal lawsuit against the project still pending.
notes: Sabin 2026 entry 4351; litigation venue: Federal, State

short_description: In January 2024, Vista Sands Solar, LLC (Vista Sands), an affiliate of Doral Renewables, proposed Vista Sands Solar, a 1,300-MW solar farm with a 300-MW battery energy storage system which would be the largest solar farm in the state.
long_description: In January 2024, Vista Sands Solar, LLC (Vista Sands), an affiliate of Doral Renewables, proposed Vista Sands Solar, a 1,300-MW solar farm with a 300-MW battery energy storage system which would be the largest solar farm in the state. The project would be located on approximately 9,500 acres of privately-owned agricultural land in the Village of Plover and towns of Grant, Plover and Buena Vista. An alliance of opponents including hunters, birdwatchers and public land advocates opposed the project and raised concerns about impacts to the greater prairie-chicken population, a threatened species. The Wisconsin Wildlife Federation intervened in the regulatory approval process asking the Public Service Commission (PSC) to reduce the project size by 20 to 30 percent to better protect the birds’ habitats. In July 2024 the PSC and the Wisconsin Department of Natural Resources issued a joint final Environmental Impact Statement (EIS) that recommended scaling back the plans by removing 10 of the proposed areas for solar arrays. The agencies had received over 400 comments on their draft EIS. In December 2024, after reviewing the developer’s detailed report of the public health, ecosystem and economic benefits of the project, the PSC unanimously approved the scaled down version of the project and described it as one of the most valuable for the state. The developer agreed to restore up to 7,900 acres of agricultural land in the vicinity of the wildlife area, to seed the area under development with a beneficial wildflower mix, and not to construct within 500 feet of important habitat for the great prairie chicken. Construction is expected to begin in late 2025 and the project is expected to produce enough electricity to power about 200,000 homes.

long_description: In July 2025, NextEra Energy proposed a 100-MW solar farm with a 50-MW battery energy storage system (BESS) to be located on approximately 1,148 acres in the Town of Morgan, Oconto County. Although the developer is seeking to have the project permitted at the state level, in October 2025, local government officials held a town hall meeting regarding the project. The majority of residents expressed their opposition to the project. Opponents, including Senator Eric Wimberger and Representative Elijah Behnke, raised concerns of loss of farmland, fire risk from batteries, and the potential future construction of data centers near the project. Representatives of the developer declined to attend the town hall meeting after receiving online threats from surrounding township residents.

short_description: In 2024, Ranger Power proposed the 180-MW Whitewater Solar project to be located on approximately 2,800 acres of farmland.
long_description: In 2024, Ranger Power proposed the 180-MW Whitewater Solar project to be located on approximately 2,800 acres of farmland. The project site includes land within the City of Whitewater and Town of Cold Spring in Jefferson County, and the Towns of Whitewater and LaGrange in Walworth County. Opponents of the project intervened in the permitting process before the Wisconsin Public Service Commission (PSC) and raised several objections, including the loss of farmland, impacts to the tourist and rural character of the community, and impacts to the nearby Kettle Moraine State Forest. In September 2025, the Wisconsin PSC unanimously approved the project. The opponents requested a second hearing before the Wisconsin PSC. In November 2025, the Wisconsin PSC issued its final decision, affirming its approval finding that the project is in the public interest, it will not have undue adverse impacts on environmental values, and it does not unreasonably interfere with the orderly use of land. The opponents launched an online campaign to raise funds for legal fees to support an appeal challenging the PSC’s decision.

short_description: The Beech Ridge Wind Farm, a 100-MW wind project in Greenbrier County, was met with local opposition when it was proposed in 2005.
long_description: The Beech Ridge Wind Farm, a 100-MW wind project in Greenbrier County, was met with local opposition when it was proposed in 2005. Opponents including the Animal Welfare Institute and Mountain Communities for Responsible Energy challenged the project before the PSC, and then in federal court. During the pendency of the federal lawsuit, the developer agreed to continue construction on only 40 out of the planned 124 turbines until a decision on the merits. In 2009, a federal district court found flaws in analysis of impacts on the endangered Indiana bat and imposed severe restrictions on the project. The court allowed the developer to complete the 40 turbines under construction but enjoined the operation of those wind turbines at all times except winter, unless the parties could agree otherwise. The project was completed in 2010 with the construction of 67 turbines.
notes: Sabin 2026 entry 4359; litigation venue: Federal

long_description: In 2005, landowners in Grant County filed a nuisance lawsuit in state court to enjoin the construction and operation of a wind power project planned by Shell WindEnergy, Inc. and NedPower. The trial court dismissed the action, holding that the state public service commission’s approval of the project deprived the court of jurisdiction to enjoin the project. The West Virginia Supreme Court reversed on appeal in June 2007, finding that the lower court had improperly dismissed the lawsuit and remanding the case back to the lower court for further proceedings. The 264-MW wind farm was completed in 2008, despite the legal challenges.

long_description: In 2025, Enel North America proposed the 100-MW Brandonville Solar project to be located on approximately 1,000 acres between Glade Run and Big Sandy Creek, about one mile north of Brandonville. In October 2025, the West Virginia Public Service Commission (PSC) opened a public comment period on the project. Opponents of the project, including State Delegate George Street, raised concerns about loss of farmland and impacts on property values and wildlife, and noted that, according to the Interconnection Field Study, the actual output of the solar farm is estimated to be about 50 percent less than proposed. In February 2026, the PSC concluded that the project is not contrary to the public interest given its positive economic impact on Preston County and the state of West Virginia, and thus granted the siting certificate. The developer has indicated that construction of the project will begin in December of 2026 and the project will be operational by the end of 2027.

short_description: In 2011, Wasatch Wind proposed a 66-turbine wind farm in Converse County.
long_description: In 2011, Wasatch Wind proposed a 66-turbine wind farm in Converse County. The project was opposed by local residents due to concerns about potential impacts to scenery, recreation, property values, and the Laramie Range wilderness. The opponents formed the Northern Laramie Range Alliance (NLRA) to organize against the project, including by advocating for zoning regulations that would prohibit wind development above an elevation of 6,000 feet; when this failed, the group appealed state and county permitting decisions and eventually took a case to the Wyoming Supreme Court. Although these efforts failed, Converse County did enact slightly stricter wind regulations. Construction was completed in 2016.

short_description: The Rail Tie Wind Project, a 26,000-acre, 504-MW wind farm proposed by ConnectGen (which was acquired by Repsol in March 2024), has experienced delays after becoming embroiled in legal controversies.
long_description: The Rail Tie Wind Project, a 26,000-acre, 504-MW wind farm proposed by ConnectGen (which was acquired by Repsol in March 2024), has experienced delays after becoming embroiled in legal controversies. At a meeting in February 2020, residents urged the county planning and zoning commission to place a moratorium on wind development to block the project, citing concerns about the potential for aesthetic changes to the classic western landscape, effects on local wildlife, and the potential for groundwater contamination during the installation of turbine foundations. An attorney representing landowners opposed to the project also lobbied the county to impose aggressive setback requirements that would effectively block wind energy projects. However, neither the moratorium nor the setbacks were implemented. While the State Board of Land Commissioners initially denied the developer’s lease application on 4,800 acres of state land in November 2020, the Board reversed its decision and approved the lease in January 2021. The Albany County Board of Commissioners then granted final approval in July 2021. Local residents and businesses challenged the permit, and, in May 2022, the Albany County district court upheld the permit. Over 45 residents signed onto an appeal to the Wyoming Supreme Court, and the Wyoming Supreme Court affirmed, upholding the permit on April 18, 2023. In December 2023, the Wyoming Department of Environmental Quality’s Industrial Siting Council approved the project, drawing a lawsuit. On December 23, 2024, the Albany County Conservancy and other plaintiffs filed a lawsuit in federal court to stop the project, alleging violations of the NEPA, the National Historic Preservation Act, and the Administrative Procedure Act. The project, if completed, is expected to produce $130 million in tax revenues

short_description: In 2018, Repsol Renewables North America began the development of the 650-MW Laramie Range Wind Project, comprising 170 wind turbines on approximately 56,000 acres 20 miles northwest of Cheyenne.
long_description: In 2018, Repsol Renewables North America began the development of the 650-MW Laramie Range Wind Project, comprising 170 wind turbines on approximately 56,000 acres 20 miles northwest of Cheyenne. The proposal faced strong local opposition, mostly from adjacent non-participating landowners. On September 16, 2025, after several weeks of public hearings, the Board of County Commissioners rejected the project with a 3-1 vote. During the public hearings, opponents of the project raised concerns about threats to wildlife, excessive noise, vibrations becoming a nuisance, obstruction of views and a decrease in property values. In November 2025, the developer sued the Laramie County Board of Commissioners in the Wyoming First Judicial Court challenging the rejection of the project on the basis that the county acted “arbitrarily and capriciously.”
notes: Sabin 2026 entry 4388; litigation venue: State

short_description: In 2022, Focus Clean Energy proposed the “Pronghorn H2” project, comprising a roughly 300 MW wind farm and 280 MW solar farm, to power a hydrogen production facility.
long_description: In 2022, Focus Clean Energy proposed the “Pronghorn H2” project, comprising a roughly 300 MW wind farm and 280 MW solar farm, to power a hydrogen production facility. The project is to be located on public and private lands spanning a total of approximately 40,000 acres near Glenrock. The project has faced strong opposition from local ranchers, landowners, and a group called “Taxpayers Against Pronghorn H2 Project.” The opponents have raised concerns over public safety, water use, viewshed impacts, impacts on wildlife migration, and interference with private property rights. In April 2025, the Wyoming State Board of Land Commissioners, in a 4-1 vote, approved a lease for the project. With the same vote, the Board also approved a lease for another project by the same developers in neighboring Niobrara County (see Sidewinder Wind). In July 2025, a local rancher filed a lawsuit in the district court challenging the state approval of the Pronghorn project. In December 2025, the district court ruled that the Board had violated its own rules by approving the lease for the project. In January 2026, the developer revised the project proposal, reducing its size to 30% of the initial footprint and indicating that it would move forward with only the wind and solar facilities and not the hydrogen production component of the project. In February 2026, the Wyoming State Board of Land Commissioners, in a 3-2 vote, rescinded the land lease for the project. Chuck Gray, Wyoming Secretary of State and the only member of the Board of Land Commissioners to initially vote against the proposals, released a statement after the vote celebrating the cancellation of “woke wind leases.”
notes: Sabin 2026 entry 4411; litigation venue: State

short_description: In 2025, Focus Clean Energy, Acciona, and Nordex Green Hydrogen jointly proposed the 1,000-MW Sidewinder H2 Wind farm on approximately 120,000 acres of private and public land in eastern Wyoming.
long_description: In 2025, Focus Clean Energy, Acciona, and Nordex Green Hydrogen jointly proposed the 1,000-MW Sidewinder H2 Wind farm on approximately 120,000 acres of private and public land in eastern Wyoming. The project has faced strong opposition from local ranchers, landowners, and a group called “Niobrara County Against Sidewinder” which maintains a website containing information and petitions opposing the project. Concerns about the project primarily relate to over public safety, water use, viewshed impacts, impacts on wildlife migration, and interference with private property rights. In April 2025, the Wyoming Board of Land Commissioners, in a 4-1 vote, approved a lease for the project. In July 2025, a local rancher filed a lawsuit in the district court challenging the state lease approval of another project by the same developers in neighboring Converse County. The district court ruled that the Board had violated its own rules by approving the lease for that project (see entry on Pronghorn Wind). In January 2026, the developers revised both the Sidewinder and the Pronghorn project proposals. In February 2026, the Wyoming State Board of Land Commissioners, in a 3-2 vote, rescinded the land leases for the two projects. Chuck Gray, Wyoming Secretary of State and the only member of the Board of Land Commissioners to initially vote against the proposals, released a statement after the vote celebrating the cancellation of “woke wind leases.”

short_description: On August 23, 2022, the Woodbury County Board of Supervisors adopted a new ordinance to increase the setback distance from wind turbines to occupied residences from 1,250 feet to 2,500 feet.
long_description: On August 23, 2022, the Woodbury County Board of Supervisors adopted a new ordinance to increase the setback distance from wind turbines to occupied residences from 1,250 feet to 2,500 feet. This reduced the buildable acreage in the county from 177 to 1.7. The change is expected to kill MidAmerican Energy’s proposed Siouxland Wind Farm. On May 22, 2023, the Woodbury County Board of Supervisors again increased the setbacks from residential areas to 2 miles and imposed a 1-mile setback from conservation areas. The required setbacks for wind would be 5 miles in either direction from byway roads, 1,500 feet from property lines, and two miles from any incorporated city. short_description: In 2017, Ford County imposed a moratorium on wind energy projects while it revised its ordinance.
long_description: In 2017, Ford County imposed a moratorium on wind energy projects while it revised its ordinance. In 2018, the county board’s zoning committee recommended increasing the existing 1,000-foot setback from buildings to 2,250 feet. At a hearing in October 2018, a group called Ford County Citizens for Property Rights demanded 3,250-foot setbacks from any property lines. On September 13, 2021, the County Board adopted an amended wind ordinance that increased setback to 2,250 feet from property lines upon which a primary structure is located. The ordinance further specified that, even if neighbors agreed to waive the setback requirement, any wind tower still must be at least 1,000 feet from the nearest primary structure. In 2023, Ford County amended its zoning rules to provide that, if the existing restrictions were “judicially determined to be invalid for any reason,” then the setbacks prescribed by Public Act 102-1123 (2023) would apply.

short_description: The Woodson County Board of County Commissioners has enacted a moratorium and prohibition on Commercial Renewable Energy Projects in the unincorporated area of Woodson County.
long_description: The Woodson County Board of County Commissioners has enacted a moratorium and prohibition on Commercial Renewable Energy Projects in the unincorporated area of Woodson County. Specifically, the resolution directs the suspension of acting on any application for a Conditional Use Permit or permits for the erection and construction of any Commercial Renewable Energy Project (Section 1), prohibits the establishment of any such project (Section 3), and declares such establishment a violation of public interest while the resolution is in effect. No applications for Conditional Use permits shall be set for public hearing prior to 12 months from adoption (Section 2). The moratorium may be extended, terminated earlier, or amended by subsequent resolution (Section 5). The resolution “shall remain in effect until the end of February 2026” (Section 6). There are no stated conditions or exceptions limiting the prohibition to specific areas, prior approvals, or compliance status. The moratorium is currently in effect as of December 5, 2025.

long_description: In September 2023, Sedgwick Country enacted a 6-month moratorium on solar applications as it considered new solar regulations. In March 2024, the Sedgwick County Commission extended the September 2023 moratorium on new commercial solar farms until September 2024. In August 2024, the county adopted new regulations, officially ending the moratorium. The new regulations prohibit solar projects from exceeding 1,500 acres in area; prohibit solar projects from being located in or on more than 6 contiguous sections of land; and require new solar projects be set back at least 2 miles from the nearest solar project.

short_description: In December 2021, the Reno County Commission banned wind development in all zoned areas of the county.
long_description: In December 2021, the Reno County Commission banned wind development in all zoned areas of the county. As of December 2021, a moratorium on commercial wind development was scheduled to run through March 2022. As of February 2023, the county’s zoning regulations provide that, “[i]n order to provide for an incorporated city to extend its corporate boundary and increase its tax base, no turbine shall be located within 1 mile of an incorporated city boundary.” Wind farms are permitted, however, in a designated Commercial Wind Energy Conversion Systems District in the unincorporated part of the county.

short_description: The City of Waltham’s zoning code effectively limited large-scale solar energy facilities to industrial zones.
long_description: The City of Waltham’s zoning code effectively limited large-scale solar energy facilities to industrial zones. A developer who owned land in Waltham and a neighboring town sought permission from the city building inspector to build an access road on the land the developer owned in Waltham to a proposed 1-MW solar facility in a neighboring town. The building inspector denied permission on the basis of local zoning restrictions. On June 4, 2022, the Supreme Judicial Court struck down the restrictions, finding that “[a]n outright ban of large-scale solar energy systems in all but one to two percent of a municipality’s land area . . . restricts rather than promotes the legislative goal of promoting solar energy” and that, “in the absence of a reasonable basis grounded in public health, safety, or welfare, such a prohibition is impermissible.”  Note that this is included as a pre-March 2022 development because the relevant restriction was in place before March 2022.

short_description: In May 2023, Pelham residents voted to amend the town’s solar and energy storage bylaws.
long_description: In May 2023, Pelham residents voted to amend the town’s solar and energy storage bylaws. The town prohibited energy storage systems as a principal use in all zoning districts and required all large-scale solar projects (defined as installations between 1.5 and 15 acres of land) to be set back at least 500 feet from nearby streets. The town further required developers to set aside 4 times the total area of a solar installation for forestland conservation, if the project would convert any existing forestland for solar development. In December 2023, the Massachusetts Attorney General’s office sent a letter to the town rejecting portions of the amended bylaw, including the forestland conservation requirement, noting that certain bylaw provisions failed to comply with state law that prohibits municipalities from banning solar installations through zoning.

long_description: Shutesbury’s solar bylaw, adopted in May 2008 and amended in June 2021, prohibits solar plants larger than fifteen acres, among other restrictions. In January 2023, Shutesbury residents voted to adopt a revised town bylaw for solar arrays at a Special Town Meeting. The revised bylaw would have banned energy storage systems as a principal use in all zoning districts and limited large-scale solar installations (defined as installations between 1.5 and 15 acres of land) to a special use in Forest Conservation Districts, prohibiting such installations in all other districts. The Massachusetts Attorney General’s office sent a letter to Shutesbury officials disapproving of the January 2023 bylaw, partially based on a determination that the bylaw violated state law by effectively banning solar installations. The Attorney General’s office’s action resulted in the pre-2023 bylaw regaining legal effect. The pre-2023 bylaw is the subject of a lawsuit filed by developer PureSky Energy in August 2023, in which PureSky alleges that the town’s solar regulations are in violation of state law that prohibits unreasonable regulation of solar energy systems.

short_description: In May 2024, residents of Northfield voted in favor of two citizen’s petitions to place 1-year moratoriums on utility-scale solar projects and battery storage facilities.
long_description: In May 2024, residents of Northfield voted in favor of two citizen’s petitions to place 1-year moratoriums on utility-scale solar projects and battery storage facilities. During the annual town meeting, proponents argued that the moratoriums would provide time for the town to draft bylaws regulating utility-scale solar projects and battery storage facilities. Opponents argued that the moratoriums would halt the town’s efforts toward clean energy. Some commenters noted that the moratorium might conflict with state law, as Chapter 40A, Section 3 of Massachusetts General Law states that “No zoning ordinance or bylaw shall prohibit or unreasonably regulate the installation of solar energy systems or the building of structures that facilitate the collection of solar energy, except where necessary to protect the public health, safety or welfare.”

long_description: In November 2015, the Town of Freedom enacted a wind turbine ordinance that requires all wind turbines be set back 2,500 feet from any Scenic or Special Resource. Depending on the height and megawatt capacity of the turbine, the ordinance requires it be setback either 1.5 times turbine height, 3 times turbine height, or 13 times turbine height from non-participating landowners. Turbines less than 100 feet in height and less than or equal to 10 kW in capacity must be set back at least 1.5 times turbine height; turbines between 100 and 150 feet in height and less than or equal to 10 kW in capacity must be set back at least 3 times turbine height; and turbines greater than 150 feet in height and/or greater than 10 kW in capacity must be set back at least 13 times turbine height. The ordinance measures turbine height by the highest point of any turbine blade tip. Shadow flicker is limited to ten hours per year, and depending on the time of day and height of turbine, noise is limited to between 30 and 40 dBa.

long_description: In 2015, Lancaster County adopted updates to its zoning code to require that wind turbines maintain noise limits of 40 dBa in the day and 37 dBa at night at non-participating dwellings. The county also set the following setback requirements: 2 times turbine height from non-participating property lines, 3.5 times turbine height from non-participating dwellings, and 2 times turbine height from participating dwellings. The county defined turbine height as hub height plus rotor radius. In 2019, Lancaster County once again updated its wind energy regulations to require a 1-mile setback from non-participating dwellings.

long_description: In May 2024, the Knox County Board of Supervisors voted 5-1 to change setback rules for wind turbines from 2,000 feet to 6,600 feet from nonparticipating dwellings. A wind energy company, which had been working to develop a 600-MW project in the county, filed a lawsuit against the county alleging that the zoning rule changes were made “with the express purpose of regulating” the wind energy company and its proposed wind project. On May 7, 2025, the Planning Commission voted to recommend a ban on commercial wind and solar development in the county. On June 11, 2025, the County Board of Supervisors voted to adopt the Planning Commission’s recommendation to ban any new commercial wind or solar projects. See entry on North Fork Wind (Knox County) for more information.

short_description: In March 2024, the Kiskiminetas Township Planning Commission began discussions to revise the Township’s Commercial Solar Energy Systems (CSES) Ordinance.
long_description: In March 2024, the Kiskiminetas Township Planning Commission began discussions to revise the Township’s Commercial Solar Energy Systems (CSES) Ordinance. On July 9, 2025, the Board of Supervisors approved the new ordinance. The new ordinance imposes a $50,000 annual development fee per 1-MW of nameplate capacity for large-scale solar projects, as well as a non-refundable $2,500 application fee. The ordinance also limits solar development to industrial zoning districts as a conditional use; and establishes 300-foot setbacks from property lines and 10-foot height restrictions.

long_description: In January 2011, the Town of North Kingstown placed a 6-month moratorium, which was extended by 90 days in June 2011. In November 2011, the Town Council voted to prohibit all wind turbines in the town pending the issuance of a state report anticipated in early 2012. The moratorium was motivated by opposition to a proposal to construct two wind turbines in the town. However, those two turbines were not subject to the moratorium. As of March 2023, wind energy systems are prohibited in the town, not including any approved prior to November 21, 2011.

long_description: In January 2015, the Northeastern Vermont Development Association (NVDA)—one of eleven Vermont regional planning commissions—unanimously approved a resolution against the development of all industrial wind energy systems. The resolution states that “[i]t is the position of the NVDA that no further development of industrial-scale wind turbines should take place in the Northeast Kingdom.” This position was reaffirmed in NVDA’s 2018 Energy Plan and in NVDA’s June 2023 memorandum readopting that plan. NVDA’s resolution is not legally binding and is intended to serve as a “starting point” for member municipalities’ zoning process. These member municipalities are Caledonia, Essex, and Orleans counties.

short_description: In April 2025, the Arkansas legislature enacted the Wind Energy Development Act (SB437) which was signed into law on April 22, 2025.
long_description: In April 2025, the Arkansas legislature enacted the Wind Energy Development Act (SB437) which was signed into law on April 22, 2025. The law became effective on August 3, 2025, though its implementing rules (adopted on January 14, 2026) are still pending Legislative Council approval. The law  created Arkansas’ first statewide permitting regime for wind energy facilities of at least 5 megawatts (MW) and exceeding 200 feet in height. The law requires a minimum setback from non-participating property lines of 3.5 times the total height of the wind turbines or 2,500 feet, whichever is greater and a 1-mile setback from a school, hospital, nursing home or church. The law provides that the noise level from wind turbines at non-participating dwellings shall not exceed 35 dBA. Among other things, the law also prohibits wind energy facilities from causing interference to radio, television, or internet reception on adjoining properties; requires developers to file insurance policies, acoustics expert reports, and financial security documentation at least 30 days before commencing construction; and requires developers to publish notice of the project at least once per week, for two consecutive weeks, within 30 days before filing the permit application.

long_description: On May 3, 2023, the state adopted a law directing the New York Power Authority (NYPA) to develop renewable energy projects “to support the state’s renewable energy goals established pursuant to the climate leadership and community protection act.” While the law generally encourages renewable energy development, it places two significant limitations on where renewable energy facilities may be sited. First, the law specifies that NYPA shall not develop renewable energy generation projects on “land used in agricultural production . . . unless [the] project is in furtherance of an agrivoltaics project” (i.e., unless the project is designed to accommodate dual-use farming and energy production). Second, the law provides that NYPA “shall . . . not build on lands located upon any Native American territory or reservation . . . except through voluntary sale or other agreement for such use with the consent of the relevant nation.”

short_description: S.B. 583, codified at W.V. Code §24-2-1o, limits utility-scale solar generation capacity in several ways.
long_description: S.B. 583, codified at W.V. Code §24-2-1o, limits utility-scale solar generation capacity in several ways. The law prohibits any single solar generation facility from having a generating capacity greater than 200 MW, and the law sets a cumulative generating capacity limit of 400 MW for all solar generation facilities “operating at any given time, and for which rate recovery is provided by the commission under this section.” The law also prohibits solar generation facilities from “hav[ing] a generating capacity greater than 50 megawatts until such time as 85 percent of that . . . facility’s annual energy output is being sold or is contracted to be sold to residential, commercial, or industrial customers pursuant to a renewable special contract or renewable tariff.” After that point, the facility’s generating capacity can expand in increments no greater than 50 MW until the facility again reaches the 85% benchmark.
